episode_title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods

stories.title: The UPI Traffic Cop Incident
stories.description: Ajay recounts being stopped by a cop in Delhi for jumping a red light. The cop refused cash, demanding digital payment, but the UPI transaction failed six times despite perfect connectivity, illustrating the fragility of a monopoly system.

stories.title: X.25 vs. TCP/IP
stories.description: Ajay compares the current push for Digital Public Goods to the 1980s networking standards war. Governments and telecom monopolies pushed for a top-down standard called X.25, while a bottom-up, robust protocol designed for battlefields (TCP/IP) by researchers and hackers eventually won out.

stories.title: PayPal's Blocked Entry
stories.description: Ajay mentions that PayPal had a 'handle' system (Amit@PayPal) working globally years ago. They wanted to launch domestic operations in India, which would have created a competitive payment landscape, but were blocked by the RBI, preventing organic innovation.

stories.title: Reading Cathedral
stories.description: Amit shares his love for Raymond Carver's short story 'Cathedral', calling it a masterpiece that 'blows his mind', and connects it verbally (though not conceptually) to Eric Raymond's essay.

core_ideas.description: True public goods (like clean air) are non-rival and non-excludable. UPI and Aadhaar are excludable, state-backed monopolies, not public goods. Calling them 'public goods' is a form of 'greenwashing' to shield them from criticism.

The belief that society can be designed top-down by experts (engineers/bureaucrats) on a whiteboard. This approach fails to account for the messiness of the real world, unlike bottom-up, self-organizing systems.

A single government standard (monopoly) creates stability but kills innovation. A messy, competitive market with rival standards (like VHS vs. Betamax or Linux distros) is healthier and drives progress.

Digital systems like Aadhaar and UPI give the state 'legibility' (visibility) into citizens' lives. Without strong checks and balances (like privacy laws), this leads to a surveillance state (Panopticon) and potential abuse of power.

India has achieved high state legibility (through technology) before achieving high state capacity or the rule of law, creating a dangerous imbalance where the state can coerce citizens but cannot effectively protect them or deliver services.

Liberty exists in a narrow corridor between state power and society's power. India's digital infrastructure risks tilting the balance too far towards the state, making it harder for society to push back.

Amit jokes that it's easy to get a Bengali 'rolling' because they are naturally round (referring to his own physique).
